newsitem.title: GERMANY: Gremany's Tietmeyer says hopes dlr correction is over.
newsitem.headline: Gremany's Tietmeyer says hopes dlr correction is over.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer was quoted on Wednesday as saying he hoped the dollar's correction against the mark had now come to an end.

Tietmeyer told Bild newspaper: "The rise of the dollar against the mark in recent weeks was a normalisation of exchange rates which has been due for a long time. I hope that this correction has now come to an end."
Tietmeyer was also quoted as saying it was particularly important at present to prevent doubts arising about the stability of the future European single currency.
"For that, uncomfortable decisions have to be taken by us as well. Depreciation pressures on the mark with inflationary consequences would be problematic."
The dollar hit a 34-month high of 1.7050 marks in European trade on Tuesday but the Tietmeyer comments helped trim the U.S. currency in Tokyo dealings.
It was quoted at 1.6835 in early European trade on Wednesday.
Tietmeyer was also quoted as saying current interest rate levels were not an obstacle to economic growth or jobs, but that he would not rule out further interest rate cuts.

"I am ruling nothing out. The central bank council will continue to watch the decisive factors for the stability of our money. But it is important to note that our interest rates are already at an historic low. From this side there are today no hindrances to growth and more jobs."

Tietmeyer also said the Bundesbank's stability-oriented policies were not to blame for Germany's current high unemployment -- which leapt by over half a million last month to a post-war record 4.66 million.
"Without the Bundesbank's stability course, we would be in far greater difficulties," he was quoted as saying.
"Our policy of stability has given the German economy very low interest rates and so has created favourable investment conditions. Therefore we will maintain our course," he said.
Tietmeyer added that this was also a good contribution to the start of the single European currency, which Germany argued must be at least as stable as the mark.
